output.name: Sekúla
output.myth: When Aun cut the string he did not cut it clean. The last of it hung from the Sun-Kite's tail, and Ennu the Kite-Wright sewed the Sun-Kite from old sailcloth for the Lamp Road. Each evening Hesk reels it in, and each morning it goes up again, which is why the sun seems to rise. One windy night the Gale Tavo took the bridle in his teeth and tore a knot loose. The head went west toward the Bailer, where the valleys ran brown, and the tail streamed east toward the Bride-Kite and caught in her ribbons. Skeru the Asking Raven saw it from the Reel and asked the wind where the string ends. The wind laughed. Tálun and Tirsa hang where the knot tore. Aun laughed when he saw it, then he was sorry, and he has been sorry since. Sil still walks the shore looking for his string. If you see a kite going up at dusk, do not call out to it. It may be carrying a dead man's name up to the Spindle.
output.finding: Start at the Bride-Kite in the east and look a little under one hand-span (about 17°) to her west, where the Sun-Kite flies along the Lamp Road.
